title: The Day Maggie Walker's Bank Took 280 Deposits, One of 31 Cents
dek: On 2 November 1903 Maggie Lena Walker opened a bank in Richmond for Black customers that white banks served badly, and took in about $8,000 on its first day.

story.company: St. Luke Penny Savings Bank (later Consolidated Bank and Trust Company)
story.event: Proposing and opening a bank for Black customers in Richmond, Virginia
story.summary: In August 1901 Maggie Lena Walker, grand secretary of the Independent Order of St. Luke, proposed that the Black mutual-aid society found a savings bank, since white banks in Richmond often refused Black customers loans or fair terms. After two years of preparation, the St. Luke Penny Savings Bank opened on 2 November 1903 with Walker as president, taking 280 deposits worth over $8,000 on its first day, against her hope of $75,000. It survived the Depression by merging into Consolidated Bank and Trust in 1930.
paragraphs: On 2 November 1903, music played and speeches were given at 900 St. James Street in Richmond, Virginia, while nearly 300 people waited to open accounts in a new bank. Its president was Maggie Lena Walker, 39, the daughter of a formerly enslaved woman, who had grown up returning her mother's clean laundry to white households. By the end of the day the St. Luke Penny Savings Bank had taken 280 deposits worth more than $8,000. Some people put in over $100; one put in 31 cents.

Walker had proposed the bank on 20 August 1901, at the convention of the Independent Order of St. Luke, a Black mutual-aid society she had led as grand secretary since it stood near bankruptcy. "Let us have a bank that will take the nickels and turn them into dollars," she told the members. She knew the conditions. White bankers in the city often would not lend to Black customers, or charged them more interest, and some refused their deposits; to keep using them, she held, merely fed "the lion of prejudice". The idea was not new: the True Reformers had received the first bank charter granted to African Americans in 1888.

It took more than two years. The order first recruited members, built a headquarters and started a newspaper. Its lawyer drew up the charter, which Virginia's Corporation Commission approved on 28 July 1903. Walker urged every St. Luke council and every member to open an account and buy stock, and the order's Grand Council took 200 shares. To prepare, she spent two hours a day studying the white-owned Merchants National Bank. Her salary as president was set at $25 a week.

She had hoped for deposits of more than $75,000. The first day brought in a little over $8,000, or $9,340.44 counting the stock sold. She was pleased, the National Park Service says, and saw the hard work ahead. She gave children penny banks; a hundred saved pennies opened an account. In 1910 the True Reformers' bank failed. Walker's survived, and in 1930, as the Depression deepened, she merged it with two other Black-owned banks to form the Consolidated Bank and Trust Company, which she chaired until her death in 1934.

quote.text: whatever we treasure for ourselves separates us from others; our possessions are our limitations. He who is bent upon accumulating riches is unable, with his ego continually bulging, to pass through the gates of comprehension of the spiritual world, which is the world of perfect harmony
quote.locator: Chapter I, "The Relation of the Individual to the Universe"
quote.source_title: Sadhana: The Realisation of Life, Project Gutenberg eBook #6842
quote.connection: Tagore warns that what we store up for ourselves walls us off from others. Walker asked thousands of people with little money to save, yet she meant savings pooled among themselves to get past a wall others had built. Whether saving can stay that open, or slowly closes a person in, the story leaves unsettled.

reflection: Walker's first day fell far short of the figure she had hoped for, and she was pleased anyway. She had spent two years, and many hours at another bank's counters, getting ready, and she counted the account of 31 cents as an account.

Tagore's warning is worth holding beside her. Saving can become a wall, and building something of your own can narrow you. Walker's answer was to build it with others and for them. You might ask the same of whatever you are putting aside now, whether money, energy or a plan: is it closing you off, or making room for more people to stand with you?
invitation: Think of one small contribution, from you or to you, that you have been treating as too little to count. Count it today: write it down, or thank the person who made it.

sources.title: Maggie Lena Walker (1864-1934)
sources.supports: Birth in 1864 to Elizabeth Draper, a formerly enslaved woman; returning laundry to white patrons as a child; elected grand secretary just before the order went bankrupt; the 20 August 1901 speech proposing a bank, newspaper and store; the bank opened in November 1903; the 1910 failure of the True Reformers' bank and the state's separation of fraternal societies from banks; the 1930 merger with two other banks to form Consolidated Bank and Trust; her death on 15 December 1934.

cross_checks.claim: The St. Luke Penny Savings Bank opened in Richmond on 2 November 1903 with Maggie Walker as president.
On the first day nearly 300 customers deposited a little over $8,000, including one deposit of 31 cents.
Walker proposed the bank at the order's convention on 20 August 1901, calling for a bank to turn nickels into dollars.
White-owned banks often refused Black customers loans or fair terms.

research_notes: First-day figures: the National Park Service gives 280 deposits totalling over $8,000 plus $1,247 of stock, $9,340.44 in all; American Heritage and American Banker give about $8,000 in deposits; some secondary pages say 'over $9,000', which is the combined figure. The story gives both the deposit figure and the combined total, and says which is which. Walker's hope of more than $75,000 is from the NPS. Merger: Encyclopedia Virginia and American Banker say the 1930 merger joined two other banks; American Heritage says three; the story uses two. Speech wording: the NPS and Encyclopedia Virginia give 'moneys'; American Heritage gives 'money' and 'take nickels'; the story quotes only the 'nickels' sentence in the NPS wording. The NPS dates the speech to 20 August 1901 and Encyclopedia Virginia agrees. 'Lion of prejudice' is a phrase the NPS attributes to Walker. The order's bankruptcy: Encyclopedia Virginia says she was elected grand secretary just before the order went bankrupt; the year is not given in the sources read, so the story gives none. Age 39 follows from her birth on 15 July 1864. Funding is marked mixed: the bank was capitalised by stock sold to the fraternal order and its members plus customers' deposits. Tagore's passage, which glosses a saying of Jesus and the Upanishads, is about spiritual life rather than banking; it is set beside the story to complicate it, not to judge Walker.
